recipe: Give a type parameter a default (`type Box<T, Unit extends string = 'px'>`) when callers almost always pass the same value, so they can omit it.
trigger_condition: You are designing a generic type where one parameter always uses the same value in practice.
evidence: Sometimes you have a value in mind for an argument and you don't want to force users of your library to constantly provide the same value over and over again. That's the situation where default arguments come in handy.
_original_recipe: Use default generic type arguments when you have a specific value in mind for a type parameter and don't want to force library users to repeatedly provide the same value.

recipe: When setting default generic type arguments, follow the same ordering rules as function parameter defaults: a required argument cannot follow a default argument.
trigger_condition: You are defining a generic type with multiple type parameters where some have defaults.
evidence: A lot of the same rules apply in types that apply to function argument defaults. For example, you can't have a required argument following a default argument.

recipe: Remember that there is no type value that behaves like JavaScript's `undefined` for function defaults; even passing `never`, `unknown`, or `any` as a type argument will be used instead of triggering the default.
trigger_condition: You are trying to omit or 'reset' a type argument to rely on its default value.
evidence: In TypeScript, even if you provide `never` or `unknown` or `any`, the value will be inserted instead of the default.

recipe: When creating a type with a complex object-like default argument, start with a literal object as the parameter default, use indexed types to handle the object shape, and add generic constraints if you encounter type errors.
